sentences.text: Hey, Andy, how you doing?
This meeting is being recorded.
Good.
Yeah, good, thanks.
How's the week been going?
Yeah, not too bad, not too bad.
Been enjoying the sunshine.
How about yourself?
Yeah, similar here.
I was ill earlier in the week and I think the sun's helped to help me recover a little bit, so.
That's always nice.
Have you only just got the flu that everybody has been having?
Yeah, I do.
I mean, I didn't know everyone was getting it and then as soon as I got it, I started hearing about everyone else getting it as well.
So I was a bit worried that I'd been spreading it to other people.
But I think you're a bit late to the party.
Actually, I had about two weeks ago, but yeah, it's killer, isn't it?
It's a long one.
Yeah.
Do you have temperature and everything?
Measure my temperature.
But certainly I felt like for the first week, the second week was kind of doable.
Yeah.
But still, I mean, it was lingering.
It wasn't one that was in and out.
It was a.
Yeah, it was pretty hard.
Glad it's gone.
Good luck.
Good luck on that.
At least it hasn't killed you.
Yeah.
So whereabouts are you based?
So we're based in London.
We work from a.
We work at the moment, the one.
The one in Victoria.
Um, I actually had a call with one of your colleagues previously.
Yeah, you spoke to Ramon.
Ramon, yeah.
So, I mean, at that point we weren't sort of really, you know, looking to sell, you know, at that point in time.
So what I basically said to him is, you know, we'll leave it for now and then come back to it maybe a bit later down the line.
So, I mean, I guess I think the main thing that we spoke about on the call when I was speaking to Ramon was the.
Your platform, so the agencies.com platform.
And he mentioned there was.
I think there was some deal that you'd been involved in with an agency in Israel that did a very thing.
Yeah, well, yeah, yeah, exactly.
So, I mean, he was sort of saying, you know, there's.
There's appetite out there for agencies in the marketing space that are sort of focused on influencer marketing.
So, I mean, I guess it's kind of.
It'd be great to get your advice on whether you think that's still something that people are looking for or, you know, what you think.
Really?
Yeah, I don't think it's.
I don't think it's going away anytime soon.
So we are seeing still a lot of activity around.
Around that space.
I Think social media agencies are still actually quite strong despite the fact that there's a proliferation of them.
But I think that's just an indicator.
There's so much work to do and I think more than ever actually people are looking to, you know, non traditional platforms to create campaigns.
So I don't think that's a big change that's going to happen anytime soon.
So there's a, an appetite for those types of transactions and also the sizes of those deals.
You know, there's big variation.

So a business of your size, if you're still relatively the same size when you spoke to Rome, would probably generate quite a bit of interest because there's not only agencies that are just a bit bigger than you that would be looking to acquire something, there's also sort of small and midsize agency groups.

And then you know, even at the bottom end of what the holding companies are looking for, they, they do look to fill gaps with, you know, agencies that are doing less than, less than 5 million in revenue.
Yeah.
As well.
So it's, I mean it's, it is an open field and there's plenty of interest.
Yeah, I mean, I suppose, I guess the main thing that makes us different from the majority of agencies is we are sort of more like a piece of software.
So it's almost, we do work as almost like a self service influence marketing tool as well for restaurants, hospitality groups, that type of thing as well.
So we're not a very sort of people heavy business.
Most of it is automated which means that obviously it's very easy to scale and also to sort of incorporate into, you know, your brand.
If you are an agency you can just take the software and you'd be able to sort of use it for your own, your own benefit as well.
How much does your clients pay them?
What do they tend to pay?
So at the moment we're changing our pricing model but basically the way that we do it is by tokens.
So the client will buy a set number of tokens.
One token is £50.
So one token will then be able to organize an influencer promotion for you.
Then we obviously do, you know, discount.
So if they bought 50, you get a, you get a discount on that.
Okay.
And what does a typical client budget for?
You know, if they're, if they're going to do a campaign on your platform.
What, what, what kind of, what's like a typical deal look like?
Yeah, I mean, so we've got one client at the moment, sort of a restaurant group with around 100 venues that they Want, but they've given us a target of 20 promotions per month.
So that's sort of their trial period.
And then they're looking to sort of expand that up to sort of 100, 200 per month.
So I'd say generally it's probably about three visits per venue.
Per month is probably our average.
Okay, I'm sorry.
So what's the typical spend there for one client?
So that would be 150 pounds per venue per month.
But obviously if the brand has, you know, 100 venues, then maybe a lot more.
So do you typically have a client that has 100 venues?
How does that normally work?
Is it usually like a one small restaurant or is it usually.
If it's a client with 100 venues, it's probably a restaurant group.
Trying to think if we've had one single company with.
With 100 venues, we've had a couple of single companies with sort of 50 to 60 venues.
I feel like maybe that leap from 60 to sort of the 100 mark is generally owned by sort of restaurant groups rather than individual companies.
Okay, cool.
But you've got this platform.
What would you have typically as well, in a sort of normal month in terms of the number of active clients on the platform?
Yeah.
So at the moment on the platform, we have.
I think we've probably got around 500 venues on there.
A lot of, well, a proportion of.
Of the clients are on sort of a free plan.

So what we do is we offer them, you know, one promotion for free each month and we're also bringing out, you know, the client portal where they'll be able to sort of see all of their information on there.
That should be ready in May.
At the moment, everything is sort of done by email.
So what's your monthly revenue then?
Do you have like a monthly recurring revenue?
This.
I don't.
I don't think that our monthly recurring revenue is sort of stable enough right now to be able to put, you know, a standard figure on that.
It goes up and down.
Feast and famine, we call it.
Yeah, typical agency.
Then, you know, you have a good period and then it'll go quiet for a while.
What have you had for the last 12 months?
You know, you're trailing 12 months.
I think I'd have to come back to you with sort of all of that in writing.
It's hard for me to give you a.
Any advice, but I don't know where you are, but just a ballpark number would be okay.
I mean, it's probably.
It's less than a hundred thousand for the year?
Yeah.
And that's total revenue?
Yeah, 100k for the year.
Are you talking about this year or you look talking about the last 12 months.
Last 12 months, yeah.
All right.
So what are you thinking at the moment?
What, what, what's the, the problem that you're trying to solve?
So I mean for us we're obviously based in the UK at the moment.
When the new version comes out it's going to allow us to expand to any country in the world and we want sort of focus on the us, the UAE and Australia.

We're also looking to get some more investment, you know, but I think the idea was potentially sort of, you know, feature the company on, on your guys platform, see if there's any interest there from any companies.

Because you know, from our perspective I feel like this is sort of a tool that a lot of marketing agencies who don't necessarily have the influencer marketing aspect might be interested in acquiring and just being able to sort of plug it into their own service.
I don't know.
What do you think?
Yeah, potentially, potentially.
So, so just to understand.
So this, the stack, the tech stack underneath is, is mainly just automations and email.
Email, like manual email to sort of join the dots between.
So there's, there's an app, a mobile app, but that's just for the influence of facing side of things.
So for example, you know, with a brand like Byron Burger or something, they might want a couple of different promotions at 10 of their venues across London.
We'll then post that for them on the app and the influencers will all be able to see that they'll be able to apply, you know, various different pieces of functionality within the app.
How many influencers do you have on the app?
We've got 6,000 at the moment across the UK.
How many are active per month?
I think it's around 2000 per month.
Okay, and what's the, what's the cost to you with the influencers?
Do you, are you paying the majority of your fees?
There's no, we don't pay the influencers anything.
The restaurants generally restaurants and hospitality venues will work with the influencers on a gifted basis.
So we're sort of, you know, the types of influences that we're working with is that sort of mid range size of influencer.
How much funding have you had so far?
It's a good question.
I'd say in terms of pure investment we've probably had around 80k.
But in terms of sort of, you know, we have some software developers that have done a lot of work for us, it probably comes to around 150k.
And what's the deal with them?
If you agree to equity for their work or how does that work?
Yeah, they're sort of working with us on a consulting basis at the moment, but then they wouldn't be eligible for any equity.
So you're paying them as they consult?
Yeah.
And how much does that investor own or the investors that are in that 80k or is that just.
Yeah, that's come from our own.
Oh, that's your own money?
Yeah, there's a.
At the moment there's only.
There's two shares in the company.
It's just me and my co founder.
So you both put the 80K in?
Yeah.
Is that friends and family or was that your own?
Cash is our own.
Wow.
Well done.
Or not, depending on whether we can get you out.
Okay, what are you looking for?
So you talked about investment we wouldn't be interested in working on.
That's somebody else.
Yes.
Yeah, definitely.
I mean, investments completely separate.
We're speaking to a lot of different potential options of people who have mentioned that this might be something they'd be interested in.

And actually from our point of view, the, the investment side is actually more from a, you know, in order to get somebody who's got more experience within the hospitality industry so that they can reach out to some of their contacts in the various different countries that we're looking to expand into.
So it would be somebody has hospitality connections in the uae, Australia, the us that would sort of be the main, the main reason for that.
Just that we can then build up our, essentially our pool of influences across those different countries as well.
And actually the, the way.

Sorry, another thing to mention is the way that we're building new version of the app where it will be available in the different regions, we're making sure that it's going to be able to be separated.
So for example, if there was interest from an agency in Australia to, you know, buy the Australian part of the app, then that's something that we could separate from the overall software.
Okay, so have you, have you explored investment yet or is, is it also new that just haven't got there yet?
Yeah, no, we, we've got, we've had some calls with a couple of venture capital firms and also a couple of angel investors, but it's very early stages.
Okay, and what, I mean, if you were to sell the business, what would you be looking for?
I suppose that's kind of, you know, what we'd be interested in sort of finding Out.

I mean if we sort of featured it on, on the platform and you know, waited to see if there was any interest, then that might be something that could give us an indicator of, you know, whether this is a point where we would want to sell it or whether we sort of hold and, and wait for a bit longer.
How long have you been doing it so far?
So we've been.
The company was set up in 2021 but I'd say we've been trading fully since 2023.
So have you got two years full accounts yet?
Yeah, we don't have accounts for this year actually the accountants still, still doing that, but we should have accounts for the this year and last year.
What do you, what do you and your partner want personally?
I mean are you both on the same page or does one of you want to leave?
You know, what's, what's the deal there?

Yeah, we're sort of on the same page in that, you know, we don't really know if we want to sell it right now, but we sort of almost want to, to see what the interest would be and whether this would be a good point sell or whether, you know, we look to invest some more into it, grow it some more and then look to sell.
Yeah.
Okay.
So from a valuation perspective, if it truly is a SAS business, which we would have to kind of look at but I guess on the face of it is you might be looking at a 3x on your revenue.
If it's an agency and a tech and agent, a tech enabled agency with 100k, I don't know what your margins are but assuming you're both taking money home, it's probably just a break even business.
So it'd be hard to give you evaluation from that perspective.
But say there was 50k of profit, normally a small business like that service business would be multiples of profits.
So it'd be something like a three or four times depending on how excited buyers got.
Maybe we could get that a bit higher.
I mean it could be that it could go up to 8 or 9 or 10 times.
Doesn't usually for a small business, but it might given that you've set up, you know, some automations that somebody could maybe plug into and plug their own channels into it and grow it.
So they might think, you know, it's better off, they're better off spending the money on acquiring this than going out and waiting 24 months for somebody to build it.

Yeah, I mean I suppose from our perspective the way that we see the value of the company is probably the sort of network of influencers that we have live on the platform and you know, maybe traction with brands, you know, recognized brands in the uk.

So I wonder, I mean, it would be good to get your advice, but do you think that maybe it would be worthwhile, you know, waiting, seeing how much traction we can sort of gain in these other countries that we're looking to sort of move into, how much bigger we can sort of build the pool of influencers and then sort of maybe looking at it again or.
Well, where are you guys?
I mean what, what's, where are you guys, you know, emotionally.
Yeah, I mean we're not, you know, we're not looking sort of cut and run and you know, do any of that.

But it's almost that, you know, we want the business to be there and visible for agencies, potential buyers, in case it's something that, you know, they suddenly think, well, you know, this is an area that we want to get into so we want it to be available for them to, to see.
But we don't necessarily, you know, we're not going to sell it just because, you know, we have to.
Yeah.
So in terms of like being realistic on the valuation.
So agencies are renowned for their acquisition models.

They've got a very established acquisition kind of economy or environment, whatever you would want to call it, you know, it's, it's been around for a long time since probably the 60s and there is just kind of a very standard way to do it.
Valuations are pretty stable over that period as well.
So most agencies sell between some of, to four to six times multiples.
That's not to say Martech businesses would, would only sell for that.
And also there's fluctuation around sexy businesses and some other bits in and out.
You know, influencers is a sexy space.
You're likely to get a couple more points than a bog standard agency.
But again it's based on multiples of ebitda, which is earnings before taxes and interest and all the other that accountants add on.
So you need to have profit to have value basically.
Yeah.
So with you two both paid out of 100k, I mean 50k is not going to take a young good looking guy very much to spend that in London.
I should imagine so.
But I'm sure both you drill through your profits in a year.
So basically there is no real profit is what I'm saying.
So it's very difficult to give you an evaluation based on that.
But agencies are notorious for sticking to those valuations.
What they don't do is they don't go out buy tech for 20 times revenue.
Yeah.
So it makes it very difficult to make your target market market.

An agency, particularly if you have expectations of a SAS multiple, it's not to say you wouldn't get a good multiple but there isn't much to multiply and even if it was a, a 3x we could be talking 300k which is not bad.
Yeah, three years.
Just one, one question is obviously, so, yeah, agencies would love to see sort of huge revenue for them.

Would they ever take into account, for example, if they have, you know, a team that's role is to do this function but you know, it takes them a lot of time and you know, they look at their costs of actually having to carry out that service.
Could they see this as maybe, you know, almost like a cost saving investment?
So it's not that it's going to be like an add on that makes them a load of extra money, but it's going to be an add on that actually saves them a lot of money.
Or is that not necessarily.
I mean you mentioned it, sort of established process.
Yeah, it is a good question.
And a lot of agency owners don't really understand what M and A is for.
So in some respects, yes, somebody would be looking to do that but you've got to remember who that person would be within an agency business.
So it's mostly people on the procurement side that would be looking at that and they have nothing to do with M and A.
So there's kind of like two completely separate, separate roads that people are on within the same big business.
So procurement guy was, would probably be thinking, God I'd love to acquire Tom's company because that's save us 500k a year and we could probably buy it for 300.
Right.
So they're thinking that the M and A team are just thinking how do we bolt on 20 million in revenue?
Okay, yeah, we have a strategic need for some, something in particular that's going to help us to continue to grow and can Tom get us that?
Can Tom get us there?
Is it worth it for us?
But again they're still going to value on what you're bringing into the business and it wouldn't be, it wouldn't be connections.

If we went to like a traditional SaaS business and we did say, okay, they've got 2,000 active users and they're worth a thousand each, then we might have a 2 million dollar or pound, probably $2 million.
Really strictly speaking, let's say we've got $2 million valuation.
1.6 million.
Right.
If that's your valuation, the buyer isn't an agency.
I could tell you now that they just do not buy stuff like that.
It's very occasional but, but generally speaking they, they don't, they're getting more into it.
But it could be that a consultancy business would be, would, would pay that.
So your big consultancy businesses would tend to look.
But you're way too small for them to bother.
They would want, they would want like 200000 users on the platform and they'd want to see that you're pulling in, you know, 5 million in.
Yeah, it's just, it's a bit too small for that.
It's big, it's too small for holding companies as well on the agency side.
So it would be small agency, but I doubt they would pay the multiples.

My advice to you would be either put it on a platform for sale where there are tech buyers that might be looking at it, but they're going to pull apart your tech and see whether it is really a SAS business or not.
So you might not end up with a completed deal there.
But I mean we wouldn't, we could value you if you were profitable and stick your own agencies and find you a ton of buyers.
I don't doubt that we will get you a ton of interest.
I mean there will be 50 signed NDAs and you can have those conversations, but it's just where you are, you know, what do you want?
Because if, if, if we have, if we all spend the time doing that knowing that they're never going to come up with the result that, that you want and it will.
A lot of those will be small time buyers, but some of them would say, do you know what, I can take a punt for 300k on this.
These guys, because they're cool and they're doing something really cool in a cool space, but you're not going to get like 3 million.
Yeah, thank you for, thanks for the advice.
I mean, I think maybe it sounds like the best thing to do.

I mean, obviously we've got the new version coming out in May, hopefully and then we're going to be looking into sort of expanding into the, the various different countries, getting a little bit more investment and sort of trying to grow it a little bit more and then maybe at that point, you know, trying to increase our profits as well.
So then maybe that would be a point where we could maybe have the discussion again.
I'm happy to speak to you whenever, but I think I can actually be more useful than that.
So I would say what you need to do now, you've basically proven, you've proven that it works because you've actually built the minimum, minimum viable product.
It's not, it's not real.
You know, you've not really like spent, you know, 400 grand on developers and three years putting it together.

You basically pull together the sort of proposed service as cheaply as possible and you've, you've shown that these chain restaurants will engage on the platform even though not everybody's paying at the moment.
You know, not everybody paid for, for Google or whatever.
You know, everything.
Everybody starts out with a, a free tier to pull in users but you've pro proven that you can engage those major high street brands.
So I think what you need to do next, you, you have your own seed money in, which is great because any investor is going to say, you know, why would I risk this money?

And I think a good answer always is, well, I've just, I put 80 grand in because they're going to think, well, these guys are serious, you know, nobody shits away, I don't know how old you are, but let's just say your mid 20s.
Nobody shits away their entire life savings in their mid 20s instead of buying a house unless they believe that they're going to create something massive.
So I think there is probably a seed round that you could pull in some investors.

But the really fortunate thing is that you're in the hospitality space and actually the hospitality space is very heavily invested by VCs and actually you don't need to roll out in every other country yet and get distracted with shiny ball ball syndrome.
You could probably continue in the UK with a UK VC who will be small time, but you don't live in San Francisco and you're not there, you know, 24 hours a day.
I've heard it's not a great place anymore.
So why don't you do that route?
I mean you can Google hospitality investors and there's a ton, there's, I mean there's a few good ones certainly that I would say you could probably speak to.
I know, I know a few different ones that I've, you know, had relationships with in the past and they're, they're extremely, extremely active in investing.
And yeah, most of their investments will be restaurants and actual physical, what could you call them?
Like they sort of invest in themes, you know, so somebody will come along go, I'm going to open up six tiki bars across the whole of the UK or whatever.
They go, yeah, Tiki's really in at the moment.

And so they, they'll throw millions at that one thing and then somebody else comes with a different theme and, and they invest in these themes and it's quite cyclical, but they did, they're, they're smart investors and they usually get the money back out, which, considering hospitality, is quite a risky thing to invest in, they're very good at it and this could be a real enhancement to what they're investing in at the moment.
It'll be relatively risk free because I should imagine, given that you're, you're very humble, that you're not going to go like, I don't want 20 million off you.

But I think if you approached one of these investment funds for hospitality and said, we need 500k now to scale it to that next level to show that the minimum Bible product works, I think they would see that as a safe punt.
And certainly you might even be able to get four or five of them to invest at that level and bring in about two and a half million.
So that's my advice to you.
I think you haven't really explored whether it works yet to make it valuable.
You've shown that it works in its smallest sense.
But the next level really is to put an investment to get to that next level.
And I don't think you probably would need a lot of money, even like one developer on Upwork, to actually flesh out the entire thing would probably cost you about 50 grand or something.
So it's really about your own salaries, your office, your, your personal assistants, your Uber bill and a couple of developers.
Yeah, I mean, so the version that we're putting out in May is, you know, it's had a group of 10 developers working on it.

They only started last week actually, but they, they're meant to be done in May and that's going to be, you know, some updates to their mobile app, but then it's also some updates, you know, with a client portal, full client portal, and then an admin panel from our side.

So there's going to be three separate portals and, and hopefully that should give us sort of enough to then be able to just keep growing the pool of influencers and, and pool of clients as well, because I think, you know, the more traction we can get with clients in various different countries and, and also just focusing in the UK too, making sure that the service is actually being provided at a good, good, good level.
I think that's the most important thing.
Yeah, I, I would say don't Go to another country.
You need to show that it, it works.
You haven't smashed it out of the park in the uk, so you, you, you would just be distracting yourself.
It would be more work.
I think what you really need to do is just double down on, on sales.
The actual tech stuff, that's great that you got it for free.
I don't know what the deal is that you got with the software people there, but you just need to sell the product.

And this is where agency owners really miss the trick because they think that just, you know, even just building something, but they think just providing a service is valuable or having a, having their own brand is valuable and it's not.
People pay for, for things that make them go, wow, you know, part of it needs to be your story and how successful you and your friend have been at creating this and building this minimum thing.
But nobody's going to get excited unless they see dollars flowing through it.
They want to see, you know, that you are the coolest kids on the block and that you're building something that everybody wants to buy into.
So I would say you need to spend every single day just building more and more sales and users into the platform.
And I'm talking about brands.
Who cares about the influencers, really?
They will flock to the platform like flies to shit.
They're just after freebies, aren't they?
So you need to get as many brands paying money.
It wouldn't have to be a lot, you know, you know, five clients a month just spending a few thousand would be enough to show that it's there.
Because what happens is the investors would recognize that once you got up to the next level, that the, the budgets go from like tens of thousands to millions.
And so they, they just need to, you know, build it up to the right point and then get it acquired into one of the major agencies who are on the 5 million tier.
And they would just be able to stuff 5 million through there instead of stuffing like, you know, 500 quid or whatever you're getting at the moment.
Yeah.
So I think that that roadway that you've started to build, that's, that's the way to go.
It'll be.
I think it'd be pointless to, to try and sell it because it's not going to give you anything that you haven't just put into the.
I mean, you're clearly capable of having 40k in profits to invest in something, so it's not going to excite you, is it?
You know.
Yeah, yeah, exactly.
I think.
Thank you.
That's that's good advice.
I think we'll continue to sort of see, see how many clients we can keep getting on, focus on the UK for now and then maybe at some point look at some other countries as well.
Well, everybody wants to be in uae.
I mean, it doesn't surprise me.
You talked about that.
It's such, such a UK half the time, isn't it?

Money is, is a lot easier in the us, but because you're not there, having, having spent a lot of time in the US myself, if you're not there, there's going to be somebody that's already doing it there exactly the same.
That's going to be the hotter thing.
And there are tons, tons and tons of hospitality VCs in the UK.
So I would, I would nail your, your presentation first with those guys and then.
Yeah, I mean, you're young.
Why don't you just move out to the west coast of America and just smash it?
Or move to Texas or Florida.
There's loads of people in Austin that are doing startups now.
California is an absolute mess.
So I would say Florida if you can go to Miami, but it's seasonal.
Texas is not so bad in terms of Austin or uae.
Yeah.
But you'll find it tricky.
The market in America is just so massive, they're taking a small sliver of that is really effective in showing that something can work and scale.
So anyway, good luck much.
That's really helpful and yeah, thank you.
Yeah, no worries, no worries.
Let me know when you're a multi billionaire.
All right, Cheers, Andy.
Good luck.

Provide a detailed report on the last 12 months of revenue to Andy Day (08:14)
Explore potential investment opportunities with hospitality-focused VCs (28:37)
summary.overview: In a recent Business Development meeting between Tom McNeile and Andy Day, the two discussed several key topics, starting with personal health updates, which included Promote's recovery from the flu. Promote then presented an overview of their London-based influencer marketing company, referencing a prior conversation with Ramon regarding their platform's market interest. Andy provided insights into the strong demand within the influencer marketing space, while Promote highlighted their unique software-based approach. They delved into revenue discussions where Promote outlined their pricing model and client budgets, and Andy inquired about the company’s monthly earnings and financial stability. The conversation shifted to expansion plans, as Promote expressed a need for investment to penetrate new markets, while Andy offered advice on valuation and investment strategies. They concluded by emphasizing the importance of focusing on sales and user acquisition, with Promote agreeing to prioritize the UK market before considering international expansion. Action items included Promote's commitment to provide Andy with a detailed revenue report for the past year and explore investment opportunities with hospitality-focused VCs.
